Phần A

1. The old theatre has a beautifully ORNATE facade covered in stone carvings and sculptures. --- ORNATE (tính từ) = được trang trí cầu kỳ, chạm khắc tinh xảo; collocation phổ biến: "an ornate facade/design", "ornate carvings"; đừng nhầm với "ornamental" (mang tính trang trí, không nhất thiết cầu kỳ).

2. The businessman's new mansion is extravagantly OPULENT, with marble floors and gold fittings throughout. --- OPULENT (tính từ) = xa hoa, lộng lẫy, phô trương sự giàu có; collocation: "an opulent mansion/interiors"; mang sắc thái phô trương hơn "luxurious" trung tính.

3. The council has finally approved the DEMOLITION of the abandoned factory next month. --- DEMOLITION (danh từ) = sự phá dỡ, đập bỏ công trình; collocation: "authorise/await the demolition", "a demolition site"; danh từ tương ứng của động từ "demolish".

4. House prices in the capital have become so ASTRONOMICAL that most young couples cannot afford to buy. --- ASTRONOMICAL (tính từ) = cao ngất trời, khổng lồ (về giá cả); collocation: "astronomical prices/costs"; đừng nhầm với nghĩa gốc "thuộc về thiên văn học".

5. Close PROXIMITY to the train station was the main reason the family chose this particular flat. --- PROXIMITY (danh từ) = sự gần gũi, sự lân cận về vị trí; cấu trúc chuẩn "in (close) proximity TO sth", không dùng "proximity WITH/OF sth".

6. The new office block was designed to be purely UTILITARIAN, with no attention paid to how attractive it looked. --- UTILITARIAN (tính từ) = mang tính thực dụng, chỉ chú trọng công năng; collocation: "a utilitarian design", "purely utilitarian"; trái nghĩa với "ornate/decorative".

7. Rising rents mean that housing AFFORDABILITY is now out of reach for many students. --- AFFORDABILITY (danh từ, không đếm được) = khả năng chi trả được; collocation: "a housing affordability crisis", "ease pressure on affordability".

8. Thousands of new DWELLINGS are being built on the edge of the city to house the growing population. --- DWELLING (danh từ) = nơi cư trú, chỗ ở; collocation: "high-density dwellings", "affordable dwellings"; trang trọng hơn "home", thường dùng trong văn viết học thuật.

9. The rundown docklands area has undergone significant urban REGENERATION over the past decade through new investment in housing and infrastructure. --- REGENERATION (danh từ) = sự tái thiết, hồi sinh khu đô thị xuống cấp; collocation: "urban regeneration", "a regeneration scheme"; trái nghĩa với "decline/decay".

10. Village houses built from local stone and timber are a classic example of VERNACULAR ARCHITECTURE, reflecting centuries of adapting to the region's climate. --- VERNACULAR ARCHITECTURE (danh từ) = kiến trúc bản địa, dựa trên vật liệu và khí hậu địa phương; collocation: "traditional/preserve vernacular architecture"; khác nghĩa "vernacular" trong ngôn ngữ học (tiếng địa phương).

11. After years of renting, my cousin finally managed to GET A FOOT ON THE PROPERTY LADDER by buying her first flat last spring. --- GET A FOOT ON THE PROPERTY LADDER (idiom) = mua được căn nhà đầu tiên, bắt đầu sự nghiệp sở hữu nhà; cấu trúc cố định, không tách rời các thành phần; đồng nghĩa "become a homeowner".

12. Once a run-down industrial neighbourhood, the area has become GENTRIFIED, pushing out many long-term residents. --- GENTRIFIED (tính từ) = đã bị "thượng lưu hóa" (khu vực trở nên đắt đỏ, thu hút người giàu); mang sắc thái phê phán (đẩy người nghèo ra khỏi khu vực), khác với "renovated" trung tính.
Phần B

1. Band 6: Many people cannot afford to buy a house these days. - Band 7: A growing number of people are struggling to get a foot on the property ladder due to rising house prices. - Band 8: So astronomical have property prices become that, for a growing swathe of the population, home ownership now lies firmly beyond reach.

2. Band 6: Old buildings in the city centre are being knocked down to make space for new towers. - Band 7: The demolition of older buildings in the city centre is making way for new high-rise towers. - Band 8: Not until decades of vernacular architecture had been sacrificed to the wrecking ball did planners begin to question whether wholesale demolition was truly the wisest path to densification.

3. Band 6: Some new buildings look nice but are not very useful for everyday life. - Band 7: Some new buildings prioritise an aesthetically pleasing design over practical, everyday functionality. - Band 8: What too many contemporary developments sacrifice, in their pursuit of an ornate, photogenic facade, is precisely the utilitarian functionality that residents rely on day to day.

4. Band 6: Living near your workplace saves a lot of time every day. - Band 7: Living in close proximity to one's workplace can save a considerable amount of commuting time. - Band 8: Were housing policy to prioritise proximity to employment hubs, the cumulative hours reclaimed from commuting would arguably outweigh almost any other urban planning intervention.

5. Band 6: Governments should help poor families find somewhere affordable to live. - Band 7: Governments should intervene to improve housing affordability for low-income families. - Band 8: Only through sustained government intervention, rather than reliance on market forces alone, can the deepening affordability crisis facing low-income households be meaningfully addressed.

6. Band 6: When an area becomes popular, poorer people often have to move away because it gets too expensive. - Band 7: When a neighbourhood becomes gentrified, long-term residents are often priced out and forced to relocate. - Band 8: So rapid is the pace of gentrification in some cities that entire communities have been displaced, exchanged for opulent apartments few of the original residents could ever afford.

7. Band 6: Building with local materials can be better for the environment than using modern methods. - Band 7: Vernacular architecture, which relies on local materials, can be more environmentally sustainable than modern construction methods. - Band 8: It is precisely this vernacular wisdom, honed over generations to suit local climate and materials, that offers a compelling low-carbon alternative to today's energy-intensive construction methods.

8. Band 6: Cities are building more tall buildings because there is not enough space. - Band 7: Cities are constructing more high-rise dwellings in response to acute land shortages. - Band 8: High-density, high-rise dwellings are proliferating as cities grapple with acute land shortages, though whether such densification genuinely eases the affordability crisis remains hotly contested.

passages.text: In the autumn of 2018, the Belgian architecture practice 51N4E completed the conversion of a six-storey postal sorting office in Brussels into 134 apartments. The shell was kept; the floor slabs, mail chutes and freight lifts were reworked rather than demolished. A standard new-build of the same volume, according to the consultancy Arup, would have emitted roughly 4,300 tonnes of carbon during construction. The Brussels project emitted, by the architects' estimate, less than a quarter of that figure. The number is contested, as such figures often are, but it has become emblematic of a quiet realignment in European housing policy: the rediscovery of adaptive reuse as a legitimate, and possibly preferable, alternative to demolition.

Adaptive reuse is not a new idea. The conversion of monasteries into mills, mills into lofts, and lofts into apartments has been a feature of dense European cities for two centuries. What has shifted, according to the architectural historian Stephen Cairns at ETH Zurich, is the underlying argument. Where mid-twentieth-century reuse was driven largely by sentiment or heritage protection, contemporary projects are increasingly justified in terms of embodied carbon, the emissions released during the manufacture of construction materials. A 2021 audit by the Royal Institute of British Architects estimated that roughly half of the whole-life carbon footprint of a typical new residential building is locked into its concrete, steel and glass before a single resident moves in. Retaining the existing structure, however imperfectly, avoids most of that initial outlay.

The economic case has proved harder to settle. Adaptive reuse projects routinely encounter the constraints of fabric they did not design: low ceiling heights, irregular floor plates, mixed-period electrical systems, and load capacities that may not match the requirements of modern services. Renske Hoogerheide, a development economist at TU Delft, has found that reuse costs in the Netherlands tend to be between five and twelve per cent higher per square metre than equivalent new-build, once contingencies are included. Yet she has also argued that the comparison is misleading. Reuse delivers occupiable housing more quickly than new-build, often by twelve to eighteen months, and that earlier income stream materially changes a project's net present value. In markets where construction inflation has outpaced rental growth, the calculation has begun to tip in favour of reuse.

Parallel to adaptive reuse, a second tradition has been gathering pace: cohousing. In its modern form the model originated in Denmark in the 1970s, where small groups of households built or commissioned developments combining private dwellings with shared kitchens, laundries and gardens. The Cohousing Research Network, an Anglophone consortium, has tracked roughly 800 projects across Europe and North America. According to its 2023 review, residents report meaningful reductions in loneliness, especially among older single adults, although outcomes vary widely with project design and turnover. The energy story is similarly mixed: shared facilities reduce per-capita appliance use, but cohousing residents also tend to occupy slightly larger total floor area per person once communal spaces are counted.

The two traditions have begun to converge. A growing proportion of new cohousing projects in Western Europe are now sited inside reused buildings, on the reasoning that an old shell offers the spatial generosity (high ceilings, deep floor plates, internal courtyards) that cohousing layouts require, while spreading the embodied-carbon savings across a larger group of households. The 2022 conversion of an aluminium-fabrication plant in Ghent into a thirty-household cohousing scheme is widely cited; its embodied-carbon analysis showed a sixty per cent reduction relative to a comparable new-build, and residents report high satisfaction. Critics note, however, that such schemes remain rare, and that they require a tolerant regulatory environment which not every jurisdiction provides.

Standing in the way, in many cities, is the legal architecture inherited from an earlier era. Building codes were drafted to govern new construction; their treatment of existing structures is often ambiguous. Fire-safety regulations may demand modifications that compromise the historic fabric, and accessibility standards may be impossible to meet without substantial intervention. The architect Dorte Mandrup has argued that codes need a dedicated "existing-building" track, calibrated to performance rather than to prescriptive new-build specifications. A handful of European jurisdictions, including Flanders and parts of Switzerland, have moved in this direction; most have not.

What the literature seems to converge on is a cautious endorsement. Adaptive reuse appears to deliver substantial carbon savings, although the exact figure depends heavily on the specific building and on how embodied carbon is accounted for. Cohousing, similarly, appears to deliver social benefits where it is carefully designed, but is no panacea. Combining the two may multiply both advantages, although the projects so far remain a statistically small set. What is unlikely to recede, given the steady tightening of carbon-reporting rules across the European Union, is the question that adaptive reuse implicitly poses: whether demolition itself should now require justification, rather than being assumed as the default.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture extends our building-science series — focusing specifically on climate-responsive architecture and the empirical performance of vernacular precedents in contemporary housing stock. [pause:5s] The conceptual scaffolding I'll draw on today is taken from the work of Professor Hina Subramaniam — that's S-U-B-R-A-M-A-N-I-A-M, no hyphen, single word, with an "m" at the very end, not an "n". Subramaniam's 2017 monograph reframed climate-responsive design from a checklist of features into what she calls "envelope intelligence theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The longitudinal monitoring cohort I'll reference today was first instrumented in 2017 — sorry, let me correct that, 2016; the published descriptive statistics in 2017 covered data collected in 2016. So whenever I refer to the baseline year, please record 2016. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note. Subramaniam's theory USED TO be operationalised with static post-occupancy surveys only, NOW the field deploys mixed-methods designs incorporating continuous indoor-environmental sensing, and from 2028 a multi-country retrofit consortium WILL be embedding occupant biometric feedback into the same data pipeline. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, mixed-methods continuous sensing. Moving to terminology. The building-skin concept Subramaniam foregrounds — a multi-layered, dynamically tunable boundary that mediates heat, light, and moisture without active mechanical input — is termed an "adaptive envelope". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: smart facade, intelligent wall, responsive skin. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Subramaniam's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is adaptive envelope — a-d-a-p-t-i-v-e envelope. So when the older literature uses smart facade or responsive skin, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what building scientists call the "vernacular adaptation continuum". When researchers describe how contemporary architects retro-fit vernacular cooling strategies into modern blocks, they sketch a graded continuum running from passive shading through cross-ventilation chimneys to evaporative courtyard cooling. So, you know, you'll see practices that lift shading fins straight from Andalusian shutters — that's passive shading. Or schemes that revive the Iranian wind-tower — that's a cross-ventilation chimney. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the vernacular adaptation continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the post-occupancy data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the three hundred dwellings we monitored across four climate zones last summer, MOST reported indoor temperatures within the comfort band without mechanical cooling — roughly seventy-two per cent. Only a few — about eight per cent — required supplementary air-conditioning, and some — twenty per cent — fell into a hybrid pattern, mechanical cooling on peak days only. So passive performance dominates numerically, but the supplementary-cooling tail, though small, is theoretically significant for grid-load forecasting. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "thermal mass lag". This refers to a temporal pattern in which heavyweight construction releases stored daytime heat several hours into the evening — sometimes shifting peak indoor temperature to ten at night. At Riverside Heights, our researchers logged sixty-seven documented mass-lag episodes across the cohort during one summer. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that retrofit insulation linearly reduces summer overheating is, frankly, not supported. Most of the dwellings in our sample did NOT show the predicted monotonic improvement as insulation thickness increased. Quite the opposite — many showed a U-shaped curve, with a performance dip around the two-hundred-millimetre threshold, because over-insulated envelopes trap nocturnal heat. So the older "thicker-is-better" hypothesis, which predicts linear improvement, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT mixed-methods continuous-sensing state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in this afternoon's seminar. I want you to focus on the post-occupancy sensing protocols specifically, not the biometric futures or the legacy survey instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: climate-responsive housing is an envelope intelligence problem, not a checklist; the technical term for the dynamically tunable boundary is adaptive envelope; passive performance dominates at roughly seventy-two per cent; and the thicker-is-better insulation hypothesis is not empirically supported. Next week we'll examine embodied carbon. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

Phía ủng hộ nhà cao tầng (high-rise):

Phía ủng hộ nhà truyền thống (houses):
•  Vườn rộng được xem là thiết yếu cho phát triển thể chất và cảm xúc của trẻ em.
•  Nhà riêng cho sự riêng tư (âm thanh, không gian) mà căn hộ không sánh được.
•  Tháp xa hoa ở khu thượng lưu hóa có thể đẩy dân cư lâu năm ra ngoài, làm trầm trọng khủng hoảng.
•  Introduction — paraphrase the two maps: the transformation of the riverside district of Greenford between 1990 and 2024.
•  Overview — a shift from a low-rise, industrial-residential mix to a denser, mixed-use enclave with better green space and transport; no specific features listed.
•  Body 1 — describe 1990: terraced houses on the north bank, park to the east, derelict factory in the south-west, single narrow road bridge.
•  Body 2 — describe the 2024 changes using past-perfect-passive: factory replaced by towers, terraces retrofitted, park enlarged, metro and footbridge added.

blocks.text: The two maps depict the wholesale transformation of Greenford, a riverside neighbourhood, between 1990 and 2024.

Overall, the area shifted from a predominantly low-rise, industrial-residential mix towards a denser, mixed-use enclave, with notable improvements in green space and transport connectivity, though arguably at the expense of its original vernacular architecture.

In 1990, the north bank of the river was characterised by rows of terraced houses, while a disused textile factory dominated the south-west and a modest community park lay to the east. The sole crossing was a single narrow road bridge.

By 2024, the factory site had been redeveloped into six high-rise apartment towers, dramatically increasing residential density. The original terraces had not been demolished but had instead been retrofitted, being converted into mixed-use blocks that may have eased pressure on housing affordability. Furthermore, the park had been expanded into a riverside greenway, and a new metro station, alongside a pedestrian footbridge, had substantially enhanced accessibility. The single road bridge, meanwhile, had been widened to cope with the heavier traffic the denser district now generated.
The two maps illustrate the comprehensive redevelopment of Greenford, a riverside district, over the thirty-four years separating 1990 and 2024.

Overall, what had been a low-rise, part-industrial neighbourhood had been recast as a dense, mixed-use enclave, with green space and transport links markedly upgraded, albeit at some cost to the area's original character.

In 1990, the north bank was lined with rows of modest terraced houses, a small community park occupied the east, and a derelict textile factory stood in the south-west corner; the river, meanwhile, was spanned by nothing more than a single narrow road bridge.

By 2024, the district had been transformed almost beyond recognition. The factory had been razed and supplanted by a cluster of six high-rise apartment towers, sharply intensifying residential density, while the terraces, rather than being cleared, had been retrofitted into mixed-use blocks. The community park had been enlarged into a sweeping riverside greenway, and connectivity had been overhauled: a new metro station had been inserted at the centre, the road bridge had been widened, and a pedestrian footbridge had been introduced alongside it. Taken together, these interventions had converted a quiet residential fringe into a far more connected urban quarter.

Về từ vựng, Band 8 nâng lên lớp từ học thuật cao cấp (intensification of land use, acoustic privacy, ornate low-rise streetscapes, gentrified districts, densification, pedestrianised plazas) cùng các cụm danh từ hoá dày đặc, vượt hẳn cách diễn đạt còn khá trung tính của Band 7. Về lập luận, Band 8 sử dụng cách rào đón (hedging) học thuật tinh vi hơn (arguably indispensable, mounting evidence, I would suggest) và kết bài bằng hình ảnh ẩn dụ "a vertical neighbourhood", giúp nâng rõ điểm Task Response và Coherence & Cohesion so với Band 7.

blocks.text: Well-designed high-rise towers achieve remarkable densification, allowing a single plot of scarce urban land to house hundreds of families who would otherwise be priced out of the city centre.
Living in close proximity to public transport, offices and schools spares residents lengthy commutes and knits communities more tightly together.
Sustainable design features such as passive ventilation and rooftop greenery can lower a building's running costs while easing its environmental footprint over decades of use.
The careful refurbishment of an ageing property can preserve its ornate period details while quietly upgrading insulation, wiring and plumbing to modern standards.
Purely utilitarian tower blocks, stripped of any concern for aesthetic appeal, can leave residents feeling that they inhabit an anonymous concrete shell rather than a home.
Uncontrolled suburban sprawl forces households into long, car-dependent commutes and saddles municipalities with the cost of extending roads, pipes and power lines ever further outward.
New-build construction generates substantial embodied carbon, since manufacturing concrete and steel releases greenhouse gases long before a single occupant moves in.
Chasing an opulent facade or lavish interior finish can quietly drive up a project's budget, leaving developers tempted to cut corners on less visible structural work.
Rapid urban migration has concentrated demand for dwellings in a handful of major cities, pushing the ratio of buyers to available homes wildly out of balance.
Speculative investment in property, rather than genuine demand for shelter, has been a significant driver behind the astronomical prices seen in many global cities.
A shortage of buildable land within city limits leaves planners with little option but to pursue densification rather than continued horizontal expansion.
Decades of underinvestment in ageing housing stock have left many neighbourhoods in need of large-scale regeneration rather than piecemeal repair.
When ordinary wage growth fails to keep pace with property values, an entire generation can find itself unable to get a foot on the property ladder.
Households that become cost-burdened by housing expenses are typically forced to cut back sharply on healthcare, education and savings.
As formerly affordable neighbourhoods become gentrified, long-term residents are often priced out and displaced to the urban periphery.
The loss of vernacular architecture to generic modern developments can leave a city's streetscape indistinguishable from countless others worldwide.
Balancing the urgent need for more dwellings against the desire to protect a neighbourhood's historic character remains a genuinely thorny planning dilemma.
Many renters feel that handing over a large share of their income each month for a property they will never own is tantamount to throwing money down the drain.
Deciding whether a crumbling structure merits costly renovation or should instead be cleared for demolition places planning authorities in an unenviable position.
Reconciling ambitious sustainable design targets with tight construction budgets continues to challenge architects working on affordable housing projects.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: Governments can rein in runaway affordability pressures by releasing more land for development and streamlining planning permission for new dwellings.
Incentivising regeneration of derelict inner-city sites, rather than permitting further suburban sprawl, allows cities to grow without swallowing yet more farmland.
Mandating stricter building codes on embodied carbon would push developers towards locally sourced, lower-impact materials from the outset.
Offering tax relief for the refurbishment of listed buildings encourages owners to restore an ornate facade rather than opting for cheaper demolition.
Many young professionals argue that high-rise apartment living, for all its compromises, is the only realistic route to independence in an expensive city.
A growing number of homeowners believe that any building lacking genuine aesthetic merit does a disservice to the streets it occupies, however functional it may be.
There is a widespread sentiment that renting will always feel less secure than owning, no matter how convenient a rented dwelling might be.
Many conservationists insist that vernacular architecture embodies irreplaceable local knowledge that no contemporary design can fully replicate.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: National and local governments bear primary responsibility for tackling the affordability crisis through coherent housing policy rather than short-term fixes.
Property developers have an obligation to weigh the risk of gentrified displacement against the profits generated by upscale regeneration projects.
Architects and engineers are best placed to champion sustainable design and to minimise embodied carbon at the drawing-board stage, before construction even begins.
Heritage bodies are responsible for identifying which structures merit protection, ensuring that valuable vernacular architecture is not lost to hasty demolition.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: Although critics dismiss high-rise living as impersonal, thoughtfully designed towers with shared gardens can foster just as strong a sense of community as any suburb.
While some regard suburban sprawl as wasteful, it could be argued that low-density housing still offers families a garden and privacy that no densification scheme can match.
It is sometimes claimed that heritage protection stifles progress, yet preserving vernacular architecture need not preclude sensitive renovation that meets modern needs.
Sceptics of sustainable design point to its higher upfront cost, but such investment is generally recouped through lower energy bills over a building's lifetime.
As land in major cities grows scarcer, densification is likely to become the default strategy, with high-rise dwellings proliferating even in traditionally low-rise districts.
Concern over embodied carbon is expected to push architects towards timber and other renewable materials in place of concrete and steel.
Continuing affordability pressures may see more households abandon the goal of ownership altogether, treating long-term renting as the new norm rather than a stopgap.
Growing public unease about gentrified neighbourhoods could prompt cities to attach stricter affordable-housing quotas to future regeneration schemes.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas previous generations could realistically expect to get a foot on the property ladder in their twenties, many young adults today remain lifelong tenants well into middle age.
Compared with a plain utilitarian block, a building that pairs sound engineering with genuine aesthetic ambition tends to age far more gracefully in the public's affection.
Unlike unchecked suburban sprawl, compact densification around transport hubs uses infrastructure far more efficiently, even if it sacrifices private garden space.
In contrast to older neighbourhoods shaped by vernacular architecture, newly built districts often display a uniform, placeless style dictated by cost rather than climate or culture.
A personal anecdote about a family that spent years renting before finally saving enough to get a foot on the property ladder illustrates the emotional weight of the affordability crisis.
Case studies of former industrial docklands transformed through urban regeneration show how derelict sites can be repurposed into vibrant, if occasionally gentrified, communities.
Photographic comparisons of a historic quarter's ornate facades alongside a nearby utilitarian tower block vividly demonstrate shifting architectural priorities over time.
Surveys of first-time buyers describing themselves as cost-burdened provide compelling evidence of how far incomes have fallen behind property prices in many cities.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: As property prices in major cities have soared, debate has intensified over whether vertical living in high-rise apartments or horizontal living in traditional houses offers the better remedy. While both models have merit, I tend to side with high-rises as the more workable response to today's housing crisis.

Supporters of high-rise apartments argue, with some justification, that vertical living makes highly efficient use of scarce urban land. A single tower can accommodate hundreds of families on a plot that would otherwise house a handful, which is arguably the only realistic answer to astronomical property prices in dense metropolises. Modern complexes also tend to include communal amenities such as gyms, gardens and round-the-clock security, and are often built close to public transport, sparing residents an exhausting daily commute.

On the other hand, proponents of traditional houses emphasise quality-of-life advantages that flats simply cannot replicate. Spacious gardens are widely regarded as essential for children's physical and emotional development, and a detached home offers a degree of privacy that no apartment can match. Critics of vertical living also point out that stacking thousands of people into glass towers can intensify a sense of disconnection from nature.

In my opinion, however, the sheer scale of the affordable housing crisis tips the balance towards high-rises. While I sympathise with the desire for a garden, it seems somewhat unrealistic to expect most young families ever to get a foot on the property ladder if cities continue prioritising low-density sprawl. Well-designed, mixed-use towers, with green roofs and communal spaces, can deliver much of what traditional homes offer without consuming valuable land.

The chronic housing shortage gripping major urban centres has reignited a long-standing architectural debate: whether to densify upwards through high-rise apartments or preserve the cultural fabric of traditional, low-rise housing. Although both camps invoke legitimate concerns, I am persuaded that vertical living represents the more defensible path forward.

Advocates of high-rise development make a compelling case grounded in spatial economics. The intensification of land use, after all, allows a single plot to accommodate hundreds of households, which, in cities where property prices have reached astronomical levels, is arguably indispensable. Behind the modern facade of such complexes lies a suite of communal amenities and, in many cases, integrated transit access, features that materially shorten commutes and lessen reliance on private vehicles. Such is the spatial efficiency of vertical living that several Asian metropolises now house entire neighbourhoods within single mixed-use developments.

Defenders of traditional houses, conversely, foreground considerations that resist easy quantification. Among these are the developmental benefits of private gardens for young children, the acoustic privacy denied to apartment dwellers, and the cultural continuity embodied in ornate, low-rise streetscapes. There is, moreover, mounting evidence that opulent towers in newly gentrified districts often displace long-term residents, exacerbating rather than alleviating the housing crisis.

In my considered opinion, however, the demographic arithmetic ultimately favours densification. It is precisely because urban land is finite, and because suburban sprawl entails unsustainable infrastructure costs, that well-designed vertical living must form the backbone of housing policy. The refurbishment of older towers and the integration of green roofs, communal courtyards and pedestrianised plazas can, I would suggest, mitigate the alienation often associated with apartment life. Done thoughtfully, the high-rise need not be a concrete monolith but rather a vertical neighbourhood capable of accommodating the modern household.

Band 7: Buildings should be designed to save energy.
→ Band 8: Sustainable design principles are increasingly being embedded into contemporary architecture.
Band 7: Old buildings should be looked after.
→ Band 8: The preservation of vernacular architecture is vital to safeguarding a community's cultural identity.
Band 7: Cities are building lots of tall apartment blocks.
→ Band 8: High-density, high-rise dwellings are proliferating as cities grapple with acute land shortages.
Band 7: Run-down areas can be made better.
→ Band 8: Urban regeneration schemes can breathe new life into neglected, derelict neighbourhoods.

The Tiny House Movement: A growing architectural and social movement that advocates for downsizing living spaces (often under 400 sq ft) to reduce financial burdens and environmental impact.
Green Architecture: Modern skyscrapers are increasingly incorporating sustainable features, such as solar panels, rainwater harvesting systems, and natural ventilation to achieve LEED certification.

2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Preserving Historic Buildings vs. Demolishing for New Housing

For Preservation: Historic buildings are tangible links to a nation's cultural heritage; their unique aesthetics and ornate facades attract tourists, boosting the local economy; once demolished, this history is lost forever.

For Demolition: Dilapidated buildings are often unsafe and highly energy-inefficient; prime city land must be utilised for vertical living to solve the affordable housing crisis; modern utilitarian designs are more practical for today's needs.
Topic: Renting vs. Buying a Home

Advantages of Buying (Mortgage): Provides long-term financial security and an asset that appreciates in value; offers psychological stability ("a roof over one's head"); allows for complete freedom in renovation.

Advantages of Renting (Tenant): Offers high geographical mobility for career changes; avoids the stress of maintenance costs and property taxes; eliminates the risk of being tied to an astronomical mortgage during an economic downturn.
Topic: Vertical Living (Apartments) vs. Horizontal Living (Houses)
Vertical Living (Pros): Highly efficient use of land in crowded metropolises; often includes shared amenities (gyms, pools) and better security; closer proximity to public transport and workplaces.
Horizontal Living (Pros): Provides spacious gardens and green areas, essential for children's development; offers greater privacy and less noise from neighbours; avoids the "concrete jungle" feeling.

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~270 words)

The building I'd like to discuss is the Sagrada Familia in Barcelona — Antoni Gaudí's still-unfinished masterpiece that I had the privilege of visiting back in 2023 during a Mediterranean tour. Even setting aside its religious significance, it stands as arguably the most extraordinary feat of vernacular architecture I have ever encountered.

Situated in the Eixample district, the basilica has been under construction since 1882 — a staggering 140-plus years — and is projected to be completed by 2026, marking the centenary of Gaudí's death. Aesthetically, the building defies straightforward description: its ornate facades depict the Nativity, Passion, and Glory of Christ in extraordinary detail, while the towering spires, eighteen in total once finished, will make it the tallest church in the world at 172 metres.

What truly took my breath away, however, was the interior. Gaudí designed the columns to branch upwards like a forest canopy, and stained glass windows cast pools of cobalt blue and amber across the nave, creating an almost otherworldly atmosphere. Rarely have I been so genuinely moved by a built environment.

Several factors make this building unforgettable for me. Firstly, it represents an unparalleled synthesis of nature, engineering, and spirituality — Gaudí drew his structural inspiration from hyperboloids and helicoids, mathematical forms he observed in tree trunks and seashells. Secondly, the fact that construction has spanned five generations speaks to a kind of intergenerational ambition we rarely see in our throwaway culture. And thirdly, what made it personally significant was witnessing how a single visionary's blueprint could be faithfully executed by successors he never met.
In essence, the Sagrada Familia is far more than a building; it's a meditation on time, faith, and human persistence rendered in stone.

blocks.text: Q1: Should housing be a right?

Point: I'd argue unequivocally that adequate housing should be enshrined as a fundamental right, though I'd be the first to acknowledge that operationalising this principle is fraught with genuine economic difficulties.

Explain: The case for housing as a right rests on the fact that shelter is a precondition for virtually every other freedom — without stable accommodation, accessing education, employment, or healthcare becomes nearly impossible. Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights already recognises this, yet implementation has been wildly inconsistent.

Example: Vienna offers what is probably the most successful real-world model: roughly 60% of residents live in social or subsidised housing, with rents capped at around €7 per square metre, and the result is that the city consistently tops global liveability rankings. Conversely, in markets where housing has been left entirely to speculative forces — like Hong Kong, where the median home costs 18.8 times annual income — the social consequences include record homelessness and plummeting birth rates.

Link: So while pure market mechanisms have plainly failed, treating housing as a right requires governments to actively build, regulate, and subsidise — not merely declare the principle and walk away.
Q2: Are skyscrapers sustainable?
Point: The sustainability of skyscrapers, contrary to popular assumption, is genuinely debatable — they're far less environmentally efficient than their proponents often claim.

Explain: The core tension is that while vertical living maximises land use efficiency, supertall buildings carry an enormous embodied carbon footprint due to the steel and concrete required, and their operational energy demands — particularly for elevators, HVAC, and water pumping — scale non-linearly with height.

Example: Research on tall-building energy use suggests that structures over 50 storeys can consume substantially more energy per square metre than mid-rise alternatives, partly due to the mechanical demands of lifts, wind-load structural reinforcement, and facade maintenance at height. The Burj Khalifa, for instance, requires roughly 250,000 gallons of water daily and an estimated $2 million annually just for facade cleaning. By contrast, Copenhagen's 8 House — a mid-rise mixed-use development by Bjarke Ingels — achieves comparable density at a fraction of the carbon cost, while incorporating green roofs and natural ventilation.

Link: This suggests that the sustainable urban form of the future is more likely to be the dense mid-rise neighbourhood — the so-called "Paris model" — rather than the iconic supertall, which is ultimately more about prestige than performance.
Q3: Will remote work change housing?

Point: Remote work is, in my view, catalysing the most significant restructuring of residential geography since the post-war suburbanisation boom — though the effects are proving more nuanced than early predictions suggested.

Explain: The fundamental mechanism is that decoupling employment from physical location dissolves the historical premium attached to expensive city-centre real estate, redistributing housing demand across previously overlooked secondary cities and rural areas.

Example: Data from Zillow shows that in 2022, US cities like Boise and Austin saw home prices rise by over 30% within 18 months, fuelled largely by remote workers fleeing San Francisco and New York. The "Zoom town" phenomenon has revitalised dozens of formerly declining communities. Vietnam has witnessed a parallel trend, with Da Nang and Hoi An becoming digital nomad hubs, attracting an estimated 25,000 foreign remote workers annually. That said, the return-to-office push by major employers since 2023 has somewhat blunted this trend.

Link: All things considered, what we're likely to see isn't a wholesale abandonment of cities but rather a more polycentric pattern — and developers who anticipate this shift by building flexible, work-from-home-friendly housing stand to benefit considerably.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Welcome back. Today I want to weave together three threads that the housing debate routinely teases apart: affordability, vernacular architecture, and sustainable design. They are, in fact, the same conversation viewed from three angles.

> Consider, first, the affordability crisis. The internationally accepted benchmark is that housing should consume no more than thirty percent of household income. By that measure, the median resident of London, Sydney or Vancouver is now severely cost-burdened — paying upwards of forty-five percent of earnings simply to keep a roof overhead. Astronomical property prices, driven by speculative investment and chronic undersupply, have effectively pulled the first rung of the property ladder out of reach. The British charity Shelter estimates that over a million households in England now face a deficit of genuinely affordable homes.

> Now, vernacular architecture — the unfashionable cousin of the design world. Indigenous Bedouin tents, Yemeni tower houses, Vietnamese stilt dwellings — these forms evolved over centuries to harvest shade, channel breeze and exploit local materials. They embody what we now rebrand as passive design: thick mud walls for thermal mass, deep eaves for solar shading, internal courtyards for cross-ventilation. Modernist contempt for the vernacular cost us a vast, climate-tuned intelligence.

> Finally, sustainable design. The conversation has matured beyond bolt-on solar panels. The contemporary frontier is embodied carbon — the emissions locked into concrete and steel during manufacture. A timber-framed dwelling, by contrast, sequesters carbon over its lifetime. The most promising path forward fuses vernacular intelligence with engineered timber, modular construction and co-housing models that share amenities and cut per-capita land use.

Table two — but hold that thought, because I want to pre-empt a comfortable conclusion. One might leave this lecture imagining that the remedy is simply to build more, build greener, build in timber, and the affordability knot loosens itself. Would that it were so. Let me complicate it with a phenomenon the housing economists call the "filtering" failure. The orthodox theory holds that new high-end construction eventually trickles down — yesterday's luxury flat becomes tomorrow's affordable rental as it ages. But empirical work, notably by the Joint Centre for Housing Studies at Harvard, finds that in supply-constrained, speculation-driven markets, filtering simply stalls. Units are bought as financial assets — sometimes left deliberately vacant — and the chain never reaches the people who need it. Building, on its own, is, um, no guarantee of affordability. [pause]

A further consideration cuts against my enthusiasm for the vernacular. There's a real danger of what we might call "heritage fetishism" — romanticising the mud-walled courtyard house while ignoring that it was often cramped, poorly sanitised, and demanded constant maintenance that few modern households can supply. The intelligence is climatic, yes, but lifting a form wholesale out of its social context risks producing handsome, uninhabitable pastiche. The task is translation, not taxidermy. [pause]

And here's a genuine tension at the heart of sustainable design that we rarely voice aloud. Embodied carbon and affordability can pull in opposite directions. Cross-laminated timber, low-carbon cements, passive-house standards — these frequently carry a green premium that, frankly, prices out the very cost-burdened households we began with. So the architect faces a trilemma: cheap, low-carbon, scalable — pick two, the saying goes. [pause]

So affordability, the vernacular and sustainability are indeed one conversation — but a conversation riddled with trade-offs no clever façade can dissolve. And resolving those trade-offs is squarely a matter of governance, not aesthetics — let me flag the key policy implication…
> The synthesis is, frankly, overdue. Now, please look at table two…

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~175 từ)
The two maps depict the wholesale transformation of Greenford, a riverside neighbourhood, between 1990 and 2024.

Overall, the area shifted from a predominantly low-rise, industrial-residential mix towards a denser, mixed-use enclave, with notable improvements in green space and transport connectivity, though arguably at the expense of its original vernacular architecture.

In 1990, the north bank of the river was characterised by rows of terraced houses, while a disused textile factory dominated the south-west and a modest community park lay to the east. The sole crossing was a single narrow road bridge.

By 2024, the factory site had been redeveloped into six high-rise apartment towers, dramatically increasing residential density. The original terraces had not been demolished but had instead been retrofitted, being converted into mixed-use blocks that may have eased pressure on housing affordability. Furthermore, the park had been expanded into a riverside greenway, and a new metro station, alongside a pedestrian footbridge, had substantially enhanced accessibility. The single road bridge, meanwhile, had been widened to cope with the heavier traffic the denser district now generated.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~197 từ)
The two maps illustrate the comprehensive redevelopment of Greenford, a riverside district, over the thirty-four years separating 1990 and 2024.

Overall, what had been a low-rise, part-industrial neighbourhood had been recast as a dense, mixed-use enclave, with green space and transport links markedly upgraded, albeit at some cost to the area's original character.

In 1990, the north bank was lined with rows of modest terraced houses, a small community park occupied the east, and a derelict textile factory stood in the south-west corner; the river, meanwhile, was spanned by nothing more than a single narrow road bridge.

By 2024, the district had been transformed almost beyond recognition. The factory had been razed and supplanted by a cluster of six high-rise apartment towers, sharply intensifying residential density, while the terraces, rather than being cleared, had been retrofitted into mixed-use blocks. The community park had been enlarged into a sweeping riverside greenway, and connectivity had been overhauled: a new metro station had been inserted at the centre, the road bridge had been widened, and a pedestrian footbridge had been introduced alongside it. Taken together, these interventions had converted a quiet residential fringe into a far more connected urban quarter.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~264 words)

As property prices in major cities have soared, debate has intensified over whether vertical living in high-rise apartments or horizontal living in traditional houses offers the better remedy. While both models have merit, I tend to side with high-rises as the more workable response to today's housing crisis.

Supporters of high-rise apartments argue, with some justification, that vertical living makes highly efficient use of scarce urban land. A single tower can accommodate hundreds of families on a plot that would otherwise house a handful, which is arguably the only realistic answer to astronomical property prices in dense metropolises. Modern complexes also tend to include communal amenities such as gyms, gardens and round-the-clock security, and are often built close to public transport, sparing residents an exhausting daily commute.

On the other hand, proponents of traditional houses emphasise quality-of-life advantages that flats simply cannot replicate. Spacious gardens are widely regarded as essential for children's physical and emotional development, and a detached home offers a degree of privacy that no apartment can match. Critics of vertical living also point out that stacking thousands of people into glass towers can intensify a sense of disconnection from nature.

In my opinion, however, the sheer scale of the affordable housing crisis tips the balance towards high-rises. While I sympathise with the desire for a garden, it seems somewhat unrealistic to expect most young families ever to get a foot on the property ladder if cities continue prioritising low-density sprawl. Well-designed, mixed-use towers, with green roofs and communal spaces, can deliver much of what traditional homes offer without consuming valuable land.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~289 words)

The chronic housing shortage gripping major urban centres has reignited a long-standing architectural debate: whether to densify upwards through high-rise apartments or preserve the cultural fabric of traditional, low-rise housing. Although both camps invoke legitimate concerns, I am persuaded that vertical living represents the more defensible path forward.

Advocates of high-rise development make a compelling case grounded in spatial economics. The intensification of land use, after all, allows a single plot to accommodate hundreds of households, which, in cities where property prices have reached astronomical levels, is arguably indispensable. Behind the modern facade of such complexes lies a suite of communal amenities and, in many cases, integrated transit access, features that materially shorten commutes and lessen reliance on private vehicles. Such is the spatial efficiency of vertical living that several Asian metropolises now house entire neighbourhoods within single mixed-use developments.

Defenders of traditional houses, conversely, foreground considerations that resist easy quantification. Among these are the developmental benefits of private gardens for young children, the acoustic privacy denied to apartment dwellers, and the cultural continuity embodied in ornate, low-rise streetscapes. There is, moreover, mounting evidence that opulent towers in newly gentrified districts often displace long-term residents, exacerbating rather than alleviating the housing crisis.

In my considered opinion, however, the demographic arithmetic ultimately favours densification. It is precisely because urban land is finite, and because suburban sprawl entails unsustainable infrastructure costs, that well-designed vertical living must form the backbone of housing policy. The refurbishment of older towers and the integration of green roofs, communal courtyards and pedestrianised plazas can, I would suggest, mitigate the alienation often associated with apartment life. Done thoughtfully, the high-rise need not be a concrete monolith but rather a vertical neighbourhood capable of accommodating the modern household.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng đảo ngữ định vị và mức độ ('Behind the modern facade... lies...', 'Such is the spatial efficiency... that...') cùng cleft 'It is precisely because... that...', trong khi Band 7 dùng cấu trúc thẳng hơn.

•  Band 8 nâng lexis lên bậc Band 8 ('intensification of land use', 'acoustic privacy', 'ornate, low-rise streetscapes', 'gentrified districts', 'densification', 'pedestrianised plazas') và nominalisation dày, vượt cụm trung tính của bản 7.

•  Band 8 lập luận tinh vi hơn với hedging học thuật ('arguably indispensable', 'mounting evidence', 'I would suggest') và kết bằng hình ảnh 'a vertical neighbourhood', nâng Task Response và Coherence một bậc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> For the average citizen, finding a home in close **proximity** to the city centre is nearly impossible due to astronomical property prices.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'proxim-' gốc Latin 'proximus' (gần nhất) → proximity = sự gần kề.
vocabulary.common_error: Cấu trúc chuẩn là 'in (close) proximity TO sth', không phải 'proximity WITH/OF sth'.
vocabulary.definition_en: closeness or nearness in space, time, or relationship
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự gần gũi, sự lân cận (về vị trí)
vocabulary.example: For the average citizen, finding a home in close proximity to the city centre is nearly impossible due to astronomical property prices.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'proxim-' gốc Latin 'proximus' (gần nhất) → proximity = sự gần kề.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mang tính thực dụng, chỉ chú trọng công năng sử dụng hơn là vẻ đẹp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The building looks boring because it was designed to be purely **utilitarian**, with a plain, concrete facade and little regard for aesthetics.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'utility' (tiện ích, công dụng) + -arian → chỉ quan tâm đến công dụng, không cần đẹp.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'utilitarian' (thực dụng, chú trọng công năng) với 'utility' (tiện ích, dịch vụ công cộng như điện nước).
vocabulary.definition_en: designed to be useful or practical rather than attractive; functional
vocabulary.definition_vi: mang tính thực dụng, chỉ chú trọng công năng
vocabulary.example: The building looks boring because it was designed to be purely utilitarian, with a plain, concrete facade and little regard for aesthetics.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'utility' (tiện ích, công dụng) + -arian → chỉ quan tâm đến công dụng, không cần đẹp.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thiết kế bền vững, hướng tới giảm thiểu tác động sinh thái của công trình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Sustainable design** principles are increasingly being embedded into contemporary architecture.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sustain' (duy trì) + design → thiết kế để môi trường được duy trì lâu dài.
vocabulary.common_error: Không dùng *sustained design* khi muốn nói thiết kế bền vững; *sustainable* và *sustained* có nghĩa khác nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: architectural practice that minimises ecological impact through energy efficiency and responsible material use
vocabulary.definition_vi: thiết kế bền vững (giảm thiểu tác động môi trường)
vocabulary.example: Sustainable design principles are increasingly being embedded into contemporary architecture.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sustain' (duy trì) + design → thiết kế để môi trường được duy trì lâu dài.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khả năng chi trả được, đặc biệt liên quan đến chi phí nhà ở.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A deepening housing **affordability** crisis has placed home ownership beyond the reach of many young adults.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'afford' (đủ khả năng chi trả) + -ability → khả năng chi trả được.
vocabulary.common_error: *Affordability* là khả năng chi trả tương đối với thu nhập, không đơn giản là giá rẻ; thường nói *housing affordability*, không *affordable ability*.
vocabulary.definition_en: the degree to which the cost of something, such as housing, is within reach of average incomes
vocabulary.definition_vi: khả năng chi trả (được)
vocabulary.example: A deepening housing affordability crisis has placed home ownership beyond the reach of many young adults.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'afford' (đủ khả năng chi trả) + -ability → khả năng chi trả được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nơi cư trú, chỗ ở của con người, dùng trang trọng hơn 'home'.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> High-density, high-rise **dwellings** are proliferating as cities grapple with acute land shortages.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'dwell' (ở, cư trú) + -ing → nơi con người 'dwell' (sinh sống).
vocabulary.common_error: 'Dwelling' là danh từ trang trọng dùng trong văn viết học thuật; trong văn nói thường ngày, 'home' hoặc 'place' tự nhiên hơn.
vocabulary.definition_en: a house, flat, or other place of residence where a person lives
vocabulary.definition_vi: nơi cư trú, chỗ ở
vocabulary.example: High-density, high-rise dwellings are proliferating as cities grapple with acute land shortages.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'dwell' (ở, cư trú) + -ing → nơi con người 'dwell' (sinh sống).

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuộc về thẩm mỹ, liên quan đến vẻ đẹp và sự đánh giá cái đẹp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The building is **aesthetically** pleasing but unfortunately not very practical.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'aesthetic' nghe gần 'esthetic/beauty' → liên quan cái đẹp.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Aesthetic' (tính từ/danh từ số ít, thuộc về thẩm mỹ) khác 'aesthetics' (danh từ, ngành mỹ học/tổng thể yếu tố thẩm mỹ).
vocabulary.definition_en: concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty; as a noun, a set of principles underlying visual style
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuộc về thẩm mỹ; (danh từ) phong cách thẩm mỹ
vocabulary.example: The building is aesthetically pleasing but unfortunately not very practical.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'aesthetic' nghe gần 'esthetic/beauty' → liên quan cái đẹp.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự cải tạo, tân trang lại một công trình cho tình trạng tốt hơn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The **renovation** of the old library will take about two years to complete.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
're-' (lại) + 'novation' liên quan 'novus' (mới, Latin) → làm mới lại.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Renovation' thường ám chỉ sửa lại toàn bộ kết cấu cũ; đừng nhầm với 'innovation' (sự đổi mới, sáng tạo).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of repairing and improving a building so that it is in good condition again
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự cải tạo, tân trang lại (công trình)
vocabulary.example: The renovation of the old library will take about two years to complete.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 're-' (lại) + 'novation' liên quan 'novus' (mới, Latin) → làm mới lại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nhà cao tầng, hoặc tính từ chỉ những công trình có nhiều tầng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> High-density, **high-rise** dwellings are proliferating as cities grapple with acute land shortages.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'high' (cao) + 'rise' (vươn lên) → tòa nhà vươn cao.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *a high-rise* như danh từ hoặc *a high-rise building* như tính từ; cần dấu gạch nối, không viết *a high rise building*.
vocabulary.definition_en: a tall building with many storeys, or relating to such buildings
vocabulary.definition_vi: nhà cao tầng
vocabulary.example: High-density, high-rise dwellings are proliferating as cities grapple with acute land shortages.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'high' (cao) + 'rise' (vươn lên) → tòa nhà vươn cao.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự tái thiết, hồi sinh một khu vực đô thị xuống cấp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Urban **regeneration** schemes can breathe new life into neglected, derelict neighbourhoods.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
're-' (lại) + 'generation' (sự sinh ra) → sinh ra lần nữa, hồi sinh khu vực cũ.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong đô thị, dùng *urban regeneration* cho tái thiết khu xuống cấp; không nhầm với *gentrification*, vốn nhấn mạnh thay đổi dân cư và nguy cơ đẩy người cũ đi.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of improving a run-down area, especially through investment in housing and infrastructure
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự tái thiết, tái sinh (khu đô thị)
vocabulary.example: Urban regeneration schemes can breathe new life into neglected, derelict neighbourhoods.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 're-' (lại) + 'generation' (sự sinh ra) → sinh ra lần nữa, hồi sinh khu vực cũ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Kiến trúc bản địa, hình thành từ vật liệu, khí hậu và văn hóa địa phương.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The preservation of **vernacular architecture** is vital to safeguarding a community's cultural identity.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'vernacular' = thuộc về bản địa → kiến trúc sinh ra từ chính vùng đất đó.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Vernacular' trong ngôn ngữ học nghĩa là 'tiếng địa phương/bản ngữ'; trong kiến trúc, nó chỉ phong cách bản địa gắn với khí hậu và vật liệu địa phương.
vocabulary.definition_en: building traditions rooted in local materials, climate and culture rather than formal architectural styles
vocabulary.definition_vi: kiến trúc bản địa (dựa trên vật liệu và khí hậu địa phương)
vocabulary.example: The preservation of vernacular architecture is vital to safeguarding a community's cultural identity.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'vernacular' = thuộc về bản địa → kiến trúc sinh ra từ chính vùng đất đó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mua được căn nhà đầu tiên, đánh dấu bước khởi đầu của việc sở hữu nhà.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It is increasingly difficult for first-time buyers to **get a foot on the property ladder**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'ladder' (cái thang) → mua nhà đầu tiên là bước đầu tiên trên chiếc thang sở hữu nhà.
collocations: get a foot on the property ladder
struggle to get on the property ladder
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm tự nhiên là *get a foot on/get on the property ladder*; không nói *put a foot in the property ladder*.
vocabulary.definition_en: to buy one's first property, marking the beginning of home ownership
vocabulary.definition_vi: mua được căn nhà đầu tiên, bắt đầu sự nghiệp sở hữu nhà
vocabulary.example: It is increasingly difficult for first-time buyers to get a foot on the property ladder.
vocabulary.headword: Get a foot on the property ladder
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'ladder' (cái thang) → mua nhà đầu tiên là bước đầu tiên trên chiếc thang sở hữu nhà.
vocabulary.pronunciation: /ɡet ə fʊt ɒn ðə ˈprɒp.ə.ti ˈlæd.ə/

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nơi trú ngụ cơ bản, một chỗ ở tối thiểu để che thân.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Even if it's a small studio, you should be grateful to have **a roof over your head**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Nghĩa đen 'mái nhà trên đầu' → chỗ ở cơ bản, tối thiểu để trú ngụ.
collocations: have a roof over one's head
provide a roof over sb's head
keep a roof over one's head
vocabulary.common_error: Khi dùng cho người cụ thể, đổi *one’s* thành tính từ sở hữu phù hợp: *a roof over my/her/their head*; thường dùng *head* số ít.
vocabulary.definition_en: basic shelter or accommodation; a place to live
vocabulary.definition_vi: nơi trú ngụ, mái nhà che thân
vocabulary.example: Even if it's a small studio, you should be grateful to have a roof over your head.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Nghĩa đen 'mái nhà trên đầu' → chỗ ở cơ bản, tối thiểu để trú ngụ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tiêu tiền lãng phí, không mang lại lợi ích hay giá trị lâu dài.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Renting an apartment feels like **throwing money down the drain**; I'd rather buy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'drain' (cống thoát nước) → tiền chảy tuột xuống cống, mất trắng.
vocabulary.common_error: Cấu trúc cố định là 'throw money DOWN the drain', không dùng 'in/into the drain'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to waste money on something that brings no lasting benefit or return
vocabulary.definition_vi: ném tiền qua cửa sổ, tiêu tiền vô ích
vocabulary.example: Renting an apartment feels like throwing money down the drain; I'd rather buy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'drain' (cống thoát nước) → tiền chảy tuột xuống cống, mất trắng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chịu gánh nặng chi phí nhà ở vượt quá tỷ lệ thu nhập hợp lý.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The median resident of London, Sydney or Vancouver is now severely **cost-burdened**, paying upwards of forty-five percent of earnings simply to keep a roof overhead.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'cost' (chi phí) + 'burdened' (bị đè nặng) → bị đè nặng bởi chi phí nhà ở.
vocabulary.common_error: Cần dấu gạch nối trong tính từ *cost-burdened households*; không dùng để chỉ mọi người có chi phí cao nếu chưa vượt tỷ lệ thu nhập đáng kể.
vocabulary.definition_en: spending an excessively high proportion of income on housing costs
vocabulary.definition_vi: chịu gánh nặng chi phí (nhà ở) quá mức
vocabulary.example: The median resident of London, Sydney or Vancouver is now severely cost-burdened, paying upwards of forty-five percent of earnings simply to keep a roof overhead.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'cost' (chi phí) + 'burdened' (bị đè nặng) → bị đè nặng bởi chi phí nhà ở.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khí thải carbon ẩn chứa trong quá trình sản xuất và vận chuyển vật liệu xây dựng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The contemporary frontier of sustainable design is **embodied carbon**, the emissions locked into concrete and steel during manufacture.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'embodied' (được chứa đựng trong) + carbon → lượng carbon "ẩn mình" bên trong vật liệu xây dựng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Embodied carbon' (phát thải từ sản xuất vật liệu) khác 'operational carbon' (phát thải từ vận hành tòa nhà, ví dụ điện, điều hòa).
vocabulary.definition_en: the greenhouse gas emissions released during the manufacture, transport and construction of building materials
vocabulary.definition_vi: khí thải carbon ẩn (phát sinh khi sản xuất vật liệu xây dựng)
vocabulary.example: The contemporary frontier of sustainable design is embodied carbon, the emissions locked into concrete and steel during manufacture.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'embodied' (được chứa đựng trong) + carbon → lượng carbon 'ẩn mình' bên trong vật liệu xây dựng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá trình tăng mật độ dân cư hoặc nhà ở trong một khu vực đô thị.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Well-designed **densification** must form the backbone of any housing policy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'dense' (dày đặc) + -ification (quá trình) → quá trình làm cho khu đô thị trở nên dày đặc hơn.
vocabulary.common_error: *Densification* là quá trình tăng mật độ đô thị; không nhầm với *density*, tức mức mật độ tại một thời điểm.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of increasing the number of dwellings or population within a given urban area
vocabulary.definition_vi: quá trình tăng mật độ xây dựng/dân cư (đô thị)
vocabulary.example: Well-designed densification must form the backbone of any housing policy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'dense' (dày đặc) + -ification (quá trình) → quá trình làm cho khu đô thị trở nên dày đặc hơn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự lan rộng vô tổ chức, mật độ thấp của các khu dân cư ra vùng ngoại ô.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Suburban sprawl** entails unsustainable infrastructure costs over time, unlike well-designed vertical living.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sprawl' = nằm dài, lan ra bừa bãi → thành phố lan rộng thiếu kiểm soát ra ngoại ô.
vocabulary.common_error: Không dùng *suburban sprawl* cho mọi sự phát triển ngoại ô; cụm này hàm ý mở rộng mật độ thấp, phân tán và thiếu kiểm soát.
vocabulary.definition_en: the uncontrolled, low-density expansion of housing and infrastructure into areas surrounding a city
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự lan rộng vô tổ chức của các khu ngoại ô
vocabulary.example: Suburban sprawl entails unsustainable infrastructure costs over time, unlike well-designed vertical living.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sprawl' = nằm dài, lan ra bừa bãi → thành phố lan rộng thiếu kiểm soát ra ngoại ô.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khu vực đã bị "thượng lưu hóa", trở nên đắt đỏ và thu hút cư dân giàu có hơn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Opulent towers in **gentrified** districts can displace long-term residents, exacerbating rather than alleviating the housing crisis.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'gentry' (tầng lớp quý tộc/thượng lưu) → khu vực bị biến thành nơi ở của người thượng lưu.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Gentrified' mang sắc thái phê phán (đẩy người nghèo ra khỏi khu vực), khác với 'renovated' vốn trung tính.
vocabulary.definition_en: describes an area that has been renovated and improved so that it appeals to wealthier residents, often displacing poorer ones
vocabulary.definition_vi: đã bị 'thượng lưu hóa' (khu vực trở nên đắt đỏ, thu hút người giàu)
vocabulary.example: Opulent towers in gentrified districts can displace long-term residents, exacerbating rather than alleviating the housing crisis.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'gentry' (tầng lớp quý tộc/thượng lưu) → khu vực bị biến thành nơi ở của người thượng lưu.
